rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Fatiha has many circulating names, but reliable Sunnah establishes only Fātihat al-Kitāb, al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī, and Umm al-Qurʾān/Umm al-Kitāb; Ibn ʿĀshūr limits discussion to these.
rows.anchor: ولم يثبت في السنة الصحيحة

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The name Fātihat al-Kitāb is established in several hadith, including the Prophet’s rule that prayer is invalid without reciting it.
rows.anchor: قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لا صلاة لمن لم يقرأ بفاتحة الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fātiha derives from fatḥ, opening by removing an obstruction to an intended place; figuratively it means the first thing, by analogy with the first person entering through a door.
rows.anchor: فاتحة مشتقة من الفتح وهو إزالة حاجز عن مكان مقصود ولوجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fātiha is not used here in its literal sense of opening; it names the beginning, either as a verbal noun or as an opener that initiates the whole.
rows.anchor: وليس مستعملا في حقيقته بل مستعملا في معنى أول الشيء تشبيها للأول بالفاتح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Forms such as bāqiya, ṭāghiya, khāṭiʾa, and ḥāqqa can function as verbal nouns; Ibn ʿAbbās glosses al-ṭāghiya as the people’s transgression.
rows.anchor: في قول ابن عباس أي بطغيانهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first thing may be called Fātiha as the object of opening, where the action first appears, or as an active participle converted into a name for the beginning.
rows.anchor: وإنما سمي أول الشيء بالفاتحة إما تسمية للمفعول بالمصدر الآتي على وزن فاعلة

rows.speaker: التفتزاني
rows.claim: Al-Taftazani says the feminine suffix shifts Fātiha from a description to a noun; Fātiha and Khātima can stand independently of any feminine noun.
rows.anchor: ولعدم اختصاص الفاتحة والخاتمة بالسورة ونحوها كانت التاء للنقل من الوصفية إلى الاسمية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By frequent use, Fātihat al-Kitāb became the conventional proper name of this sura.
rows.anchor: ثم أضيف إلى الكتاب ثم صار هذا المركب علما بالغلبة على هذه السورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fātiha is first in the Prophet’s reading order, not the first revelation; sound, widespread reports make al-ʿAlaq the first revealed passage, after which God ordered Fātiha to lead recitation.
rows.anchor: فالذي نجزم به أن سورة الفاتحة بعد أن نزلت أمر الله رسوله أن يجعلها أول ما يقرأ في تلاوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Sūrat Fātiḥat al-Kitāb, general-to-specific annexation is acceptable when both terms are generic nouns and the broader term is shortened by adding the narrower one; convention makes it idiomatic.
rows.anchor: تحسن إذا كان المضاف والمضاف إليه اسمي جنس وأولهما أعم من الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He also allows Sūrat Fātiḥat al-Kitāb as an annexation of a described noun to its adjective: a sura characterized as the opener of the Book.
rows.anchor: ويصح عندي أن تكون إضافة السورة إلى فاتحة الكتاب من إضافة الموصوف إلى الصفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Annexing Fātiha to the Book is a true relation: here the Book means the rest of the Qur’an apart from this sura, like a preface belonging to a work.
rows.anchor: وأما إضافة فاتحة إلى الكتاب فإضافة حقيقية باعتبار أن المراد من الكتاب بقيته عدا السورة

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Al-Bukhari’s Book of Medicine reports that Abu Saʿid al-Khudri used Umm al-Qurʾān in a cure for a stung person; the account includes a fuller story.
rows.anchor: ما في صحيح البخاري في كتاب الطب أن أبا سعيد الخدري رقى ملدوغا فجعل يقرأ عليه بأم القرآن

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A sound hadith calls a prayer deficient when Umm al-Qurʾān is not recited.
rows.anchor: كل صلاة لم يقرأ فيها بأم القرآن فهي خداج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Umm means the origin or source of a thing, which explains the title Umm al-Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: ووجه تسميتها أم القرآن أن الأم يطلق على أصل الشيء ومنشئه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation of Umm al-Qurʾān is that Fātiha begins the Qur’an and is therefore like a mother as origin and source of what follows.
rows.anchor: أنها مبدؤه ومفتتحه فكأنها أصله ومنشؤه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation is that Fātiha gathers the Qur’an’s three central aims: praise, commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning; the rest elaborates them.
rows.anchor: أنها تشتمل محتوياتها على أنواع مقاصد القرآن وهي ثلاثة أنواع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commands and prohibitions guide people toward well-being in both abodes; knowing the divine Commander and hoping for reward while fearing punishment complete the rationale for the Qur’an’s central aims.
rows.anchor: ولما توقفت الأوامر والنواهي على معرفة الآمر وأنه الله الواجب وجوده خالق الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation is that Fātiha compresses all Qur’anic theoretical knowledge and practical rulings, including creed, prophecy, admonition, stories, worship, transactions, ethics, and legal manners.
rows.anchor: أنها تشتمل معانيها على جملة معاني القرآن من الحكم النظرية والأحكام العملية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its phrases map onto those aims: praise covers divine perfection, Lord of the worlds divine acts, the merciful names legislation, Master of Judgment the Hereafter, worship and aid religion, and guidance human conduct and past peoples.
rows.anchor: يشمل أصول التشريع الراجعة للرحمة بالمكلفين

rows.speaker: عز الدين بن عبد السلام
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbd al-Salām distinguishes outward bodily practice as Sharia from inward heart practice as reality; worship expresses Sharia and seeking help expresses reality, together establishing servitude.
rows.anchor: { فإياك نعبد } شريعة { وإياك نستعين } حقيقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The path of those favored points to the exemplary past of communities and individuals; the final phrase evokes stories and details of misguided nations recounted in the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: يشير إلى أحوال الأمم والأفراد الماضية الفاضلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fātiha gives the reciter a general grasp of the Qur’an and invites fuller study according to capacity; this is why it is recited in every prayer rakʿa.
rows.anchor: ولأجل هذا فرضت قراءة الفاتحة في كل ركعة من الصلاة حرصا على التذكر لما في مطاويها

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد ابن المعلى
rows.claim: In al-Bukhari, the Prophet identifies al-Ḥamdu lillāh as the seven oft-repeated verses and the mighty Qur’an given to him.
rows.anchor: أن رسول الله قال الحمد لله رب العالمين هي السبع المثاني والقرآن العظيم الذي أوتيته

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī dissents from the seven-verse count and says Fātiha has eight verses.
rows.anchor: إلا الحسن البصري فقال هي ثمان آيات

rows.speaker: الحسين الجعفي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥusayn al-Juʿfī is reported to count six verses in Fātiha.
rows.anchor: الحسين{[2]} الجعفي فقال هي ست آيات

rows.speaker: بعض الناس
rows.claim: An unspecified group is reported to count nine verses; that count requires excluding the basmala and combining two other verse units.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض الناس تسع آيات ويتعين حينئذ كون البسملة ليست من الفاتحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mathānī has several possible morphological analyses; all derive from pairing a second with a first, and the verse is called repeated because it is recited in every rakʿa.
rows.anchor: ووجه الوصف به أن تلك الآيات تثنى في كل ركعة كذا في الكشاف

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: A view attributed to ʿUmar says the verses are repeated because another sura is joined to them in each rakʿa; Ibn ʿĀshūr considers this sound.
rows.anchor: وهو مأثور عن عمر بن الخطاب

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A sound hadith from ʿĀʾisha says prayers were first prescribed as two rakʿas, then travel prayer remained so while resident prayer was lengthened; Ibn ʿĀshūr uses this to explain the title.
rows.anchor: فإن الصلوات فرضت ركعتين ثم أقرت صلاة السفر وأطيلت صلاة الحضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes mathānī as repetition in prayer generally, supported by Arabic use of dual forms for repeated action and by the Qur’an’s recurrent stories and themes.
rows.anchor: وقيل لأنها تثنى في الصلاة أي تكرر فتكون التثنية بمعنى التكرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Fātiha is called mathānī because it descended twice, in Mecca and Medina, is very remote: the sura is agreed to be Meccan, making a second descent pointless.
rows.anchor: وقيل سميت المثاني لأنها ثنيت في النزول فنزلت بمكة ثم نزلت في المدينة وهذا قول بعيد جدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fātiha opens the suras as a preface to a speech or book, while its summary of Qur’anic aims makes it a rhetorically apt introduction.
rows.anchor: وهذه السورة وضعت في أول السور لأنها تنزل منها منزل ديباجة الخطبة أو الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority agree Fātiha is Meccan; the author’s preferred chronology is al-ʿAlaq, then al-Muddaththir, then Fātiha.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنه نزل قبلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other accounts place Sūrat Nūn wa-l-Qalam and al-Muzzammil before Fātiha.
rows.anchor: نزل قبلها أيضا { ن~ والقلم }

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say Fātiha was the first complete sura revealed, in contrast to al-Qalam, which they regard as having come in fragments.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم هي أول سورة نزلت كاملة

rows.speaker: بعض العلماء
rows.claim: Some scholars conclude Fātiha descended when prayer became obligatory, so Muslims recited it in prayer from the outset.
rows.anchor: وقد حقق بعض العلماء أنها نزلت عند فرض الصلاة فقرأ المسلمون بها في الصلاة عند فرضها

rows.speaker: جابر بن زيد
rows.claim: A report attributed to Jābir ibn Zayd places Fātiha fifth in the order of sura revelation.
rows.anchor: وقد عدت في رواية عن جابر بن زيد السورة الخامسة في ترتيب نزول السور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its later revelation does not conflict with its first position: once enough Qur’an existed to form a Book, Fātiha was revealed as its preface.
rows.anchor: ولا يناكد ذلك نزولها بعد سور أخرى لمصلحة اقتضت سبقها قبل أن يتجمع من القرآن مقدار

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Ṣaḥīḥayn report has God divide the prayer between Himself and the servant, answering each recited passage from praise through the request for guidance.
rows.anchor: قسمت الصلاة نصفين بيني وبين عبدي فنصفها لي ونصفها لعبدي ولعبدي ما سأل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This report confirms seven verses arranged as three, one, and three.
rows.anchor: فهن ثلاث ثم واحدة ثم ثلاث

rows.speaker: أهل المدينة
rows.claim: Medinan verse-counting does not count the basmala and treats anʿamta ʿalayhim as a separate verse.
rows.anchor: فعند أهل المدينة لا تعد البسملة آية

rows.speaker: أهل مكة وأهل الكوفة
rows.claim: Meccan and Kufan counting treats the basmala as a verse and anʿamta ʿalayhim as part of the following verse.
rows.anchor: وعند أهل مكة وأهل الكوفة تعد البسملة آية

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī counts both the basmala and anʿamta ʿalayhim as separate verses.
rows.anchor: والحسن البصري عد البسملة آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Basmala is a coined noun formed by blending letters from bismi and Allāh; naḥt creates a compact expression from a frequently spoken phrase.
rows.anchor: البسملة اسم لكلمة باسم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic used blending for ambiguous affiliations, such as ʿabshamī from ʿAbd Shams; later speakers extended the method to shorten common phrases.
rows.anchor: كما قالوا في النسبة إلى عبد شمس عبشمي خشية الالتباس بالنسب إلى عبد أو إلى شمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poets al-Rāʿī and ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa attest basmala as a verb for saying bismillah; common usage extended it to the full phrase despite omitted letters.
rows.anchor: لقد بسملت ليلَى غداةَ لقيتُها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic forms the regular verbal noun basmala and the active participle from basmala; no passive participle is attested.
rows.anchor: فشاع قولهم بسمل في معنى قال بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: المطرز
rows.claim: Al-Muṭarriz lists coined verbs for formulae including basmala, sabḥala, ḥayʿala, ḥawqala, ḥamdala, halala, jaʿala, ṭayqala, and damʿaza.
rows.anchor: الأفعالُ التي نحتت من أسمائها سبعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims agree the basmala is Qur’anic because it occurs in Solomon’s letter; beginning important acts with it is also established, though the cited hadith is described as ḥasan and is not in the Sunan or Mustadrak.
rows.anchor: هو لفظ قرآني لأنه جزء آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report that any important matter begun without the basmala is cut off is described as ḥasan, though major Sunan and Mustadrak compilers did not include it.
rows.anchor: كل أمر ذي بال لا يبدأ فيه بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم فهو أقطع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most scholars say early muṣḥaf scribes wrote the basmala at every sura except Barāʾa; its presence at Fātiha’s beginning is undisputed but is not itself a sura divider.
rows.anchor: وقال الجمهور إن البسملة رسمها الذين كتبوا المصاحف في أوائل السور ما عدا سورة براءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dispute concerns whether Qur’anic status recurs at sura openings, not whether the basmala is Qur’an at all; Ibn Rushd al-Ḥafīd makes this distinction.
rows.anchor: كما أشار إليه ابن رشد الحفيد

rows.speaker: مالك والأوزاعي وفقهاء المدينة والشام والبصرة
rows.claim: Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, and jurists of Medina, Syria, and Basra hold that the basmala is not a verse at sura openings, though it is part of the verse in Sūrat al-Naml.
rows.anchor: إلى أنها ليست بآية من أوائل السور لكنها جزء آية من سورة النمل

rows.speaker: الشافعي وأحمد وإسحاق وأبو ثور
rows.claim: One view of al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Abū Thawr, and most Meccan and Kufan jurists counts it as a verse at the start of Fātiha only.
rows.anchor: إلى أنها آية في أول سورة الفاتحة خاصة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن المبارك والشافعي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mubārak and al-Shāfiʿī’s view judged more authentic by Ibn ʿĀshūr count it as a verse at the beginning of every sura.
rows.anchor: إلى أنها آية من كل سورة

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: No direct statement is transmitted from Abū Ḥanīfa; al-Zamakhsharī inferred that he did not regard it as part of the suras, an inference Ibn ʿĀshūr accepts.
rows.anchor: عن أبي حنيفة من فقهاء الكوفة فيها شيء

rows.speaker: الباقلاني
rows.claim: Al-Bāqillānī argues proof of Qur’anic status would require mass transmission, which would preclude disagreement, or solitary reports, which would make the Qur’an probabilistic and invite claims of textual alteration.
rows.anchor: لو كانت التسمية من القرآن لكان طريق إثباتها إما التواتر أو الآحاد

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī adds that disagreement itself shows it is not Qur’an, since the Qur’an is not disputed.
rows.anchor: يكفيك أنها ليست من القرآن الاختلاف فيها

rows.speaker: عبد الوهاب
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Wahhāb argues the Prophet conveyed Qur’an uniformly and publicly; had the basmala belonged to Fātiha he would have made that clear, excluding secret or missing Qur’an.
rows.anchor: فلو كانت البسملة من الحمد لبيّنها رسول الله بيانا شافيا

rows.speaker: الغزالي
rows.claim: Al-Ghazālī replies that denying the basmala’s Qur’anic status faces the same transmission dilemma; its written Qur’anic script weakens the presumption of non-Qur’anic status, so proof is needed.
rows.anchor: إن كون التسمية مكتوبة بخط القرآن يوهن كونها ليست من القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects al-Ghazālī and al-Rāzī’s reply as question-begging: it ultimately relies on the basmala’s written placement, which requires separate examination.
rows.anchor: إذ قد صار مرجع استدلال الغزالي وفخر الدين إلى رسم البسملة في المصاحف

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: In the Muwattaʾ report of God dividing prayer, the response begins after the servant says al-ḥamdu lillāh; Mālik uses the omission of the basmala as evidence.
rows.anchor: ووجه الدليل منه أنه لم يذكر بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: In a Muwattaʾ and Ṣaḥīḥayn report, the Prophet asks Ubayy how he opens prayer; Ubayy recites from al-ḥamdu lillāh through the end without the basmala.
rows.anchor: فقرأت { الحمد لله رب العالمين } حتى أتيت

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar began recitation with al-ḥamdu lillāh and did not mention the basmala at the beginning or end.
rows.anchor: فكانوا يستفتحون بالحمد لله رب العالمين لا يذكرون

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports that the Prophet began prayer with the takbīr and began recitation with al-ḥamdu lillāh.
rows.anchor: كان رسول الله يستفتح الصلاة بالتكبير والقراءة بالحمد الله رب العالمين

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مغفل
rows.claim: Ibn Mughaffal reports that he heard none of the Prophet, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, or ʿUthmān say the basmala, and advises beginning with al-ḥamdu lillāh.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن مغفل قال

rows.speaker: أهل المدينة
rows.claim: The author calls continuous Medinan mosque practice decisive: the Prophet, caliphs, Companions, and scholars did not recite the basmala aloud in public prayers, a practice he considers mass-transmitted.
rows.anchor: فإن المسجد النبوي من وقت نزول الوحي إلى زمن مالك صلى فيه رسول الله والخلفاء الراشدون

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr adds a reliable marfūʿ report from ʿĀʾisha on the first revelation: the angel said Read, then recited al-ʿAlaq without first saying the basmala.
rows.anchor: فلم يقل فقال لي بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An Arabic-style argument against making the basmala a Fātiha verse is the close repetition of al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm in a short passage, which weakens eloquence.
rows.anchor: وذلك يوجب أن يتكرر لفظان وهما

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī answers that Qur’anic repetition can emphasize meaning and that affirming God’s mercy is especially important.
rows.anchor: إن التكرار لأجل التأكيد كثير في القرآن وإن تأكيد كونه تعالى رحمانا رحيما من أعظم المهمات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects the emphasis reply: the context has no reason for repetition, certainty of mercy is not denied, and close repetition is disfavored in eloquent speech.
rows.anchor: ولأن شأن التوكيد اللفظي أن يقترن فيه اللفظان بلا فصل

rows.speaker: البيضاوي
rows.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī says repeating the two attributes explains why God deserves praise; al-Salkūtī presents this as a reply to the Hanafi repetition objection.
rows.anchor: وأجاب البيضاوي بأن نكتة التكرير هنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr finds al-Bayḍāwī’s answer inadequate: if the repeated attributes are needed to explain praise, removing them from the basmala would avoid repetition more directly.
rows.anchor: فدفع التكرير يقتضي تجريد البسملة التي في أول الفاتحة من هاتين الصفتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the view that the basmala opens every sura as a verse, Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers the argument that identical openings everywhere violate the rhetorical art of varying openings.
rows.anchor: أن تكون فواتح سور القرآن كلها متماثلة وذلك مما لا يحمد في كلام البلغاء

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A report that Fātiha has seven verses, the first being the basmala, is cited for the Shāfiʿī position; it appears in al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī, below Ṣaḥīḥ status.
rows.anchor: ما روى أبو هريرة أن النبيء عليه الصلاة والسلام قال

rows.speaker: أم سلمة
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet recited Fātiha and counted the basmala with al-ḥamdu lillāh as a verse; al-Ṭaḥāwī objects that Ibn Abī Mulayka did not hear Umm Salama, and another report from him conflicts.
rows.anchor: وقول أم سلمة قرأ رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم الفاتحة

rows.speaker: زكرياء شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: Zakariyyāʾ notes the cited wording is not the transmitted wording; other versions only show that the basmala is a verse by itself, not that it belongs to Fātiha.
rows.anchor: على أن شيخ الإسلام زكرياء قد صرح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Agreement that everything between the muṣḥaf’s covers is Qur’an proves the basmala is Qur’anic, which is uncontested; it does not prove it must be recited at each written opening.
rows.anchor: فالجواب أنه لا يقتضي إلا أن البسملة قرآن وهذا لا نزاع فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If early Muslims also wrote sura names and Meccan or Medinan labels, writing is no proof that the basmala belongs at each opening; the single-color ink evidence defeats a colored-ink theory.
rows.anchor: المشاهد في مصاحف السلف أن حبرها بلون واحد

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas’s report in al-Bukhārī that the Prophet elongated the basmala does not establish verse status: the reciting and elongating pronouns refer to Anas, who gives it as a familiar example.
rows.anchor: وإنما جاء بالبسملة على وجه التمثيل لكيفية القراءة لشهرة البسملة

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mubārak and al-Shāfiʿī cite Muslim’s report that the Prophet recited the basmala before Sūrat al-Kawthar after God revealed it.
rows.anchor: فقرأ بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم { إنا أعطيناك الكوثر }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr argues this report does not say the basmala is part of the sura: it can be the opening formula, understood as an omitted request for refuge in God’s name.
rows.anchor: بل افتتح بها عند إرادة القراءة لأنها تغني عن الاستعاذة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If this interpretation is refused, Anas contradicts his other report that he never heard the Prophet say the basmala in prayer, so the reports would conflict fatally.
rows.anchor: لزم اضطراب أنس في روايته اضطرابا يوجب سقوطها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr’s preferred account is that the basmala was written to separate suras, make the muṣḥaf’s transitions fitting, and avoid a separator made of non-Qur’anic wording.
rows.anchor: أنها كتبت للفصل بين السور ليكون الفصل مناسبا لابتداء المصحف

rows.speaker: عثمان بن عفان
rows.claim: In a report authenticated by al-Tirmidhī, Ibn ʿAbbās asks ʿUthmān why al-Anfāl and Barāʾa were joined without a basmala; ʿUthmān says their similar subject and the Prophet’s silence led him to join them.
rows.anchor: وكانت براءة من آخر ما أنزل من القرآن وكانت قصتها شبيهة بقصتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr infers that the basmala was added between suras only when the Qur’an was assembled in ʿUthmān’s single muṣḥaf, not in Zayd’s separate sheets under Abū Bakr.
rows.anchor: إلا حين جمع القرآن في مصحف واحد زمن عثمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers agree to say the basmala when beginning any sura except Barāʾa, regardless of whether their juristic school counts it as a verse.
rows.anchor: فإن القراء اتفقوا على قراءة البسملة عند الشروع في قراءة سورة من أولها غير براءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers who do not count it as a verse may recite it at a sura opening as a recommended act of blessing that imitates the muṣḥaf scribes; this practice does not prove their legal position.
rows.anchor: فتكون قراءتهم البسملة أمرا مستحبا للتأسي في القراءة بما فعله الصحابة الكاتبون للمصحف

rows.speaker: ورش وابن عامر وأبو عمرو وحمزة ويعقوب وخلف
rows.claim: Warsh in his best-known transmission, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, Yaʿqūb, and Khalaf omit the basmala between suras; they treat its script as marking the beginning, not separation.
rows.anchor: لا يبسملون بين السورتين وذلك يعلل بأن التشبه بفعل كتاب المصحف خاص بالابتداء

rows.speaker: قالون وابن كثير وعاصم والكسائي وأبو جعفر
rows.claim: Qālūn, Ibn Kathīr, ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī, and Abū Jaʿfar recite the basmala between suras except between al-Anfāl and Barāʾa, following inherited recitation practice.
rows.anchor: يبسملون بين السورتين سوى ما بين الأنفال وبراءة

rows.speaker: مؤرج السدوسي
rows.claim: Al-Jāḥiẓ tells of al-Muʾarrij al-Sadūsī restoring the basmala before Barāʾa after hearing a phrase about the Commander returning rights; if true, Ibn ʿĀshūr treats it as a joke.
rows.anchor: فرجع مؤرج إلى مصحفه فرد على براءة بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Recitation traditions do not settle juristic rulings: readers transmit how teachers read, while prayer practice follows legal reasoning; regional alignment between readers and jurists reflects shared local learning.
rows.anchor: وليست مذاهب القراء بمعدودة من أدلة الفقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Ibn ʿĀshūr follows Mālik’s view that the basmala is not a verse at the start of al-Baqara, he explains it here because earlier commentators made this customary.
rows.anchor: كان حقا علينا أن لا نتعرض لتفسيرها هنا وأن نرجئه إلى الكلام على قوله تعالى في سورة النمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The governed element after bi is omitted, here understood as I read; omission is conventional because the basmala accompanies the beginning of good deeds and the intended action supplies the cue.
rows.anchor: متعلق المجرور في { بسم الله } محذوف تقديره هنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase is a mobile adverbial dependent on an omitted verb, not a stable predicative adverb; the specific action, rather than a generic begin, is understood.
rows.anchor: فالمجرور ظرف لغو معمول للفعل المحذوف ومتعلق به وليس ظرفا مستقرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted verb should name the action being begun, so all of that action is associated with God’s blessing; a generic begin would cover only its first instant.
rows.anchor: هي الفعل المشروع فيه المبدوء بالبسملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic and Arabic examples show context supplies omitted actions: Pharaoh’s magicians act by his might, while wedding greetings and travel formulas omit their intended verbs.
rows.anchor: قول سحرة فرعون عند شروعهم في السحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted verb precedes the basmala as in normal word order; al-Zamakhsharī’s postposed estimate, which could suggest restriction, is unjustified because no exclusivity is intended.
rows.anchor: وإذ قد كان المتعلق محذوفا تعين أن يقدر في موضعه متقدما على المتعلق به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Omitting the action makes the formula concise and reusable before any deed without altering Qur’anic wording; omitted elements differ from stable adverbs whose governors are never expressed.
rows.anchor: وقد أسعف هذا الحذف بفائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ means association or accompaniment, also including attachment; this is its commonest sense and offers a fuller blessing than construing it as an instrument.
rows.anchor: هي المصاحبة ، وهي الإلصاق أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noun ism denotes a word assigned to a particular concrete or abstract entity, whether an individual or a kind.
rows.anchor: والاسم لفظ جعل دالا على ذات حسية أو معنوية بشخصها أو نوعها

rows.speaker: أئمة البصرة
rows.claim: Basran grammarians derive ism from sumūw, elevation, since names often denote things esteemed; its original form had a final weak wāw deleted for ease or frequent use.
rows.anchor: وجعله أئمة البصرة مشتقا من السمو وهو الرفعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forms asmāʾ, asāmī, sumayy, and sammaytu support a weak final wāw; Ibn ʿĀshūr says these inflections make the Basran morphology stronger.
rows.anchor: وأن الفعل منه سمَّيْت ، وهي حجج

rows.speaker: أبو خالد القناني
rows.claim: A rajaz line by Abū Khālid al-Qanānī uses suman for name; Ibn Yaʿīsh doubts it proves the form, while ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm appeals to its written ya.
rows.anchor: واللَّهُ أَسْمَاكَ سُمًى مُبارَكاً *** آثَرَكَ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr favors the Basran derivation on morphological evidence; spelling does not establish pronunciation, while the Kufan account has stronger semantic motivation.
rows.anchor: ورأي البصريين أرجح من ناحية تصاريف هذا اللفظ

rows.speaker: الكوفيون
rows.claim: Kufan grammarians derive ism from wasm, mark, because a name is a sign; they say initial wāw was dropped and hamzat al-waṣl preserves the form.
rows.anchor: وذهب الكوفيون إلى أن أصله وسم بكسر الواو لأنه من السمة وهي العلامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Kufan counterargument that Basran forms arose through metathesis is unlikely: it violates the default and would not persist across inflections; morphology reveals original and altered letters.
rows.anchor: وأجيب عن ذلك بأن هذا بعيد لأنه خلاف الأصل وبأن القلب لا يلزم الكلمة في سائر تصاريفها

rows.speaker: ابن حزم
rows.claim: Ibn Ḥazm calls both derivations false inventions and ism a non-derived word; Ibn ʿĀshūr condemns this as reckless and cites the instruction to ask learned people.
rows.anchor: وزعم ابن حزم في كتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bismillah says in the name of God, not by God, because it marks the deed as monotheistic practice and associates it with God’s name rather than invoking His essence.
rows.anchor: وإنما أقحم لفظ اسم مضافا إلى علم الجلالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In sacrifices and actions seeking blessing or aid, scripture uses the name of God and in the name of your Lord; the name accompanies the deed, while by God would imply appeal to divine power.
rows.anchor: وكالأفعال التي يقصد بها التيمن والتبرك وحصول المعونة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commands to glorify God’s name mean to say Glory be to God, whereas commands to glorify Him mean declaring His essence and attributes free of imperfection.
rows.anchor: أَمْرٌ بتنزيه ذاته وصفاته عن النقائص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s name functions like a tribe’s identifying brand or an army’s recognized slogan, signaling affiliation with the one Lord.
rows.anchor: فاستعمال لفظ الاسم في هذا بمنزلة استعمال سمات الإبل عند القبائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The full basmala means: I read in a way accompanied by the blessing of this blessed name.
rows.anchor: أقرأ قراءة ملابسة لبركة هذا الاسم المبارك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic may use ism for the named thing itself, insert it redundantly to mean peace, or use it as a metonym for proving a referent exists. None explains the basmala.
rows.anchor: فهذه اطلاقات أخرى ليس ذكر اسم الله في البسملة من قبيلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr conjectures that the elongated bāʾ was first written in Solomon’s letter to mark its opening, then copied as a sign of a new discourse at sura beginnings.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر لي أن الصحابة لما كتبوا المصحف طولوها في سورة النمل

rows.speaker: البيضاوي
rows.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī says the supplicant names God’s essence to show aid is sought from Him, then invokes al-Raḥmān for His favors and al-Raḥīm for further reasons discussed later.
rows.anchor: يذكر علم الذات إشارة إلى استحقاقه

rows.speaker: محمد عبده
rows.claim: Muḥammad ʿAbduh proposes that the Islamic opening counters Christian formulas invoking Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: one God’s multiple names are attributes, not multiple beings; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it subtle if the premise is true.
rows.anchor: فجاءت فاتحة كتاب الإسلام بالرد عليهم موقظة لهم بأن الإله الواحد وإن تعددت أسماؤه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr suspects the formula continues Abrahamic monotheist practice: Abraham invokes the Merciful and the compassionate, and Solomon opens his letter with the basmala, likely inheriting that prophetic tradition.
rows.anchor: والمظنون أن سليمان اقتدى في افتتاح كتابه بالبسملة بسنة موروثة من عهد إبراهيم
